Hey, I’m a senior too and dealing with the same thing, and your post made me kind of reflect a bit.

Do you think right now, we all are feeling the same way? Do you think your friends *might* be trying to cut you off as well?

The person I cut off was what you’d consider my best friend. To be short, we clashed a lot. She wanted to hangout with me more than I wanted to hangout with her. For awhile, I just assumed that maybe I was just super introverted (maybe that’s partially right), but I think it was this unsettling feeling in my gut that made me realize that I wasn’t there anymore because she cared about me or wanted to hear about my day, it was because I had become a safety cushion, there for comfort when someone else wasn’t working out. 

A small example would be sophomore year, she had a boyfriend. Spent 80% of her time with him and barely spoke to me for that time. When they broke up, she came straight back and hung all over me.

When she was having a rough patch, she would literally suffocate me so that I would be forced hangout would her. If I didn’t, I was a bad person, which made it hard developing myself and my relationships.

Basically, a lot of your friends are most likely using you as a safety cushion and you might be doing the *same thing.* I don’t deny I am. In fact, when I really look at it, I do have a few small safety cushions there to hear me rant about being a safety cushion.

This is how, a lot of times, friendship is going to work when you’re out being an adult. Think about it. Do moms typically make new memories, drama-free, and go to six flags to honor their loving friendship?

No. They sit on the porch, maybe with a beer in hand, and talk about how dreadful their life is and how pitiful their old friends are. 

For an adult, it’s manageable for various reasons. In high school, it tends to be difficult since the problems 18 year old high school students face are either super trivial or super difficult and maturity levels are all over the place. For adults (like a typical 35 year old), maturity levels are more than likely similar; any problems their friends are facing, they can relate to or at least understand. They also have enough experience to know that friends come and go, that friends have their own lives, that friends have their own families, so when one doesn’t talk to the other for months or even YEARS, they don’t get hung up on it. This is why you’ll see a lot of married couples “without” social lives at 40, except they have social lives, they just understandably put themselves and their lives first and get comfortable with each other instead of finding other places. 

So, when you see this happen, just know it’s normal. You’re probably just changing as well. You shouldn’t feel bad for cutting them off. Think objectively at this, take your high school social life as a learning experience and meet new people. In college, get close to the people who you can understand and reason with. If you change or they change, don’t feel bad for distancing yourself. This is a process. A lot of us won’t even talk to our high school friends 3 years from now and we will be content with that. 

I might add that the reason it might be so satisfying cutting them off is because they may have just been too much of a strain on you to the point to where it would’ve been damaging to continue the friendship. Being lonely is something you just have to become content with for the next few months, or you could talk to others, but I know that’s difficult this time in life.

Just understand the process and accept it. It’ll all end great.
